A putting green on a Kenansville ranch lot

Requests for a backyard green are rarer out toward Kenansville than for a lawn or a dog run, but when one comes in, the acreage common to this part of the county gives it more open ground to work with than most in-town lots allow. The price does not change for the extra room: $14–$30 a square foot, priced the same this September.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

An unusual request, priced the same as anywhere else

We get far fewer putting-green calls out toward Kenansville than we do closer to Kissimmee, simply because full-time ranch and rural households ask for one less often than a subdivision homeowner does. When the request does come in, the price and the build are identical to a green in town: the same $14–$30 a square foot, the same hand-shaped base and cup-setting process. What is different is scheduling, since a job this far out usually rides along with another rural Osceola County stop rather than a standalone visit. A ranch owner asking for one is more often thinking of a small practice surface near the house than a full course-style layout, since the rest of the property already has more open ground than most backyards could offer for actual golf.

Why a green's shaped base is harder to build in the rain

Hand-shaping a Kenansville green's tiers depends on rock that holds the contour it's compacted into, and wet material from a rainy-season storm doesn't hold a shape the way properly moistened, dry-weather fill does, since oversaturated rock shifts back toward flat under the next pass of the compactor. A flat lawn base tolerates a wetter working window better than a green's tiers do, which is part of why a green's build often needs more weather buffer scheduled into June through September than a plain lawn conversion of similar size. Shaping the final tier contours on a drier day, even if base rock went down earlier in wetter conditions, protects the design.

A green near a Lake Marian fish camp

A handful of properties near town sit along Lake Marian or a connecting canal, more oriented around a dock and a boat than a manicured lawn. A green on one of these lots still keeps the state's 10-foot waterbody setback, the same as any turf near the water, and the flatter ground right along the shoreline sometimes makes for an easier build than a lot with more grade change, so long as the buildable area is confirmed against the actual shoreline first. A fish camp lot also tends to see more casual foot traffic in bare feet or wet boots fresh off a boat than a typical backyard does, which argues for a denser, better-stabilized fiber over the cheapest option in the range, even though the base and shaping steps stay the same.

Why stimp speed depends on following the maker's numbers, not a house habit

Reaching a specific stimp reading on a Kenansville green depends on matching the fiber manufacturer's own infill rate and grooming instructions for that particular nylon or polyethylene product, rather than applying the same roughly one to two pounds per square foot habit used across a lawn. Two installers using the same fiber but different infill weights or grooming patterns can hand off greens that stimp noticeably differently even though both look identical on delivery day. Asking which manufacturer's numbers a green was built to, and confirming infill was measured rather than eyeballed, is the more reliable way to predict how it will actually play.

A small green behind a lake-adjacent home

Say you have a 500 sq ft area behind a home near Lake Marian, set back well past the state's 10-foot line, and want a single-tier green with a fringe collar rather than anything elaborate. At $14–$30 a square foot, that project prices between $7,000 and $15,000 installed. Because the surrounding soil holds water longer than ridge sand does, part of that price covers building the low tier's drainage capacity a touch deeper than the same design would need on higher, faster-draining ground. A simple single-tier design like this also keeps shaping labor lower than a multi-tier layout would, which is part of why it lands toward the lower half of that range rather than the top.

Setting cups once the base is fully shaped

Cups go in after the Kenansville green's base has been shaped, compacted, and confirmed to hold its breaks, cored through at the design's marked locations rather than positioned by eye during installation. Each cup gets set and edged individually, which takes longer per hole than any other single step in building a green, since a slightly crooked or poorly seated cup stands out immediately against a surface built for precision. Waiting until the base is finished before coring also avoids having to patch a cup location that turns out to sit in the wrong spot once the shape is complete.

Low-E glass near a pool-cage green

Greens built inside or beside a screened pool cage are common in Kenansville, and a west-facing sliding door or low-emissivity window nearby is worth checking before finalizing the layout, since reflected sunlight from that kind of glass can soften turf enough to damage it. The fringe around a green, made from polyethylene that starts to give around 175 to 200°F, is more exposed to this risk than the nylon putting surface itself, which tolerates heat somewhat better. A scorched patch along one edge of an otherwise undamaged green usually traces back to exactly this kind of reflection.

Excavating a green above a shallow water table

The flatwoods and prairie soil under most Kenansville-area lots holds water closer to the surface than the sand under a Lake County ridge lot does, which matters more on a green than on a flat lawn since a green's shaped base runs four to six inches deep instead of two to four. Building the lowest tier with extra drainage capacity, rather than assuming the surrounding ground will simply carry water away on its own the way faster-draining ridge sand would, keeps a shaped green from holding water in its low corner after a summer storm. That extra planning happens once, at the design stage, rather than as a fix after the first rainy season shows where a green actually holds water, which is a cheaper place to solve the problem than digging up a finished tier later.

Rinsing a green for heat, dust, and grooming

A hose rinse on a Kenansville green does double duty: it drops surface temperature 30 to 50 degrees for more comfortable play on a hot afternoon, and it clears dust and pollen that would otherwise interfere with a clean, consistent roll. Rinsing before a grooming pass, rather than after, also helps the brush move infill more evenly, since damp infill settles differently than dry infill does under a stiff brush. This small sequencing choice, rinse first, then groom, makes routine maintenance slightly more effective without adding any extra steps to the routine itself.

Questions people ask

Is it worth installing a putting green this far from Kissimmee?

It is workable, though we see far fewer requests for one out here than for a lawn or a dog run. Pricing and the build are identical to a green closer to town; the main difference is that a Kenansville job typically gets scheduled alongside another rural stop rather than on its own.

Does a lakefront lot near Lake Marian limit where a green can go?

Yes, the same way any Florida lake works. Turf, a green included, has to stay 10 feet clear of the water's edge unless a seawall is already doing that separating, so the buildable area begins at that line rather than at the property boundary.
